lead: A power device fails as soon as one of its limits is crossed, even for microseconds. Datasheet ratings are those limits; protection keeps the device inside them. A snubber beside the switch limits the rise of voltage or current, a fuse clears faults before the surge limit is passed, and the gate drive gives clean, isolated, firm gate pulses.
prereq: You need: the turn-on and turn-off behaviour of the SCR, MOSFET and IGBT chapters.

head: Rating
Symbol
Meaning
rows: Repetitive peak off-state and reverse voltage
voltage the device may block every cycle
current at a stated case temperature
peak of one half-cycle (10 ms at 50 Hz) fault current
energy measure of a short surge, for choosing the fuse
turn-on current rise; off-state voltage rise

blocks.text: Absolute maximum ratings are limits, not working values, so designs derate: steady voltage about 60 % to 70 % of the rating, current well under the rated value, junction temperature 20 °C or more below T<sub>j(max)</sub>. A fuse protects the device only if its clearing I²t is below the device's I²t rating. di/dt matters in an SCR because conduction starts in a small area beside the gate; dv/dt matters because junction capacitance current can turn a device on.

Series devices need a resistor across each for steady voltage sharing and an R-C across each for sharing during switching; parallel SCRs need matched devices or small series inductors, while MOSFETs share naturally.

A turn-off (R-C) snubber is a capacitor C<sub>s</sub> across the switch with a resistor R<sub>s</sub> in series. At turn-off the load current I flows into C<sub>s</sub>, so the switch voltage rises at dv/dt = I / C<sub>s</sub> and the switch loss falls. At the next turn-on C<sub>s</sub> discharges through R<sub>s</sub>, which limits the peak to V / R<sub>s</sub>; the discharge, about 3 R<sub>s</sub> C<sub>s</sub>, must finish within the shortest on-time. A diode across R<sub>s</sub> (polarised snubber) lets C<sub>s</sub> charge directly.
Cs = I / (dv/dt), PRs = ½ Cs V² fs

where C<sub>s</sub> is in farads, I the current at turn-off (A), dv/dt the allowed rate of rise (V/s), V the off-state voltage (V), f<sub>s</sub> the switching frequency (Hz) and P<sub>Rs</sub> the average power in R<sub>s</sub> (W). The snubber moves loss from the switch to R<sub>s</sub>; it does not remove it.

A turn-on snubber is a small inductor L<sub>s</sub> in series with the switch. It limits the current rise to di/dt ≈ V / L<sub>s</sub>, so L<sub>s</sub> ≥ V / (di/dt rating). At turn-off its stored energy needs a path, a diode and resistor across L<sub>s</sub>; without it the inductor produces a voltage spike across the switch. Thyristors usually need both: L<sub>s</sub> for di/dt and R-C for dv/dt.

A gate driver turns a logic signal into the gate current the device needs, isolates control from power, and holds the gate firmly off. The high-side switch of a bridge has its source or emitter moving with the output, so its drive needs isolation: an optocoupler (passes a DC level, needs an isolated supply), a pulse transformer (fast, but no long pulses) or an isolated driver IC. A bootstrap capacitor, charged while the low-side switch is on, is the cheap high-side supply.

where V<sub>on</sub> and V<sub>off</sub> are the driver's on and off voltages (V), R<sub>g</sub> the external gate resistor and R<sub>drv</sub> the driver's output resistance (Ω). The driver must supply Q<sub>g</sub> in a few tens of nanoseconds, so peak currents of 1 A to several amperes are normal.

R<sub>g</sub> sets the speed: small R<sub>g</sub> gives fast edges and low loss but high dv/dt and ringing; large R<sub>g</sub> is quiet but slow and lossy. When the other switch of a bridge turns on, Miller current C<sub>gd</sub> dv/dt flows into the off device's gate; a negative off-voltage (−5 V to −8 V for IGBTs) or a Miller clamp keeps it below threshold.

examples.question: An IGBT switches 10 A off a 400 V DC link at 20 kHz, with a duty ratio of at least 0.25. Its voltage rise must be limited to 500 V/µs. Design an R-C turn-off snubber: find C<sub>s</sub>, the energy and power to be dissipated, and R<sub>s</sub> if the discharge current at turn-on is to be at most 2 A. Check the discharge time.
steps: C<sub>s</sub> = I / (dv/dt) = 10 A ÷ (500 × 10<sup>6</sup> V/s) = 2 × 10<sup>−8</sup> F = 20 nF.
Energy stored at turn-off: E = ½ C<sub>s</sub> V² = 0.5 × 20 × 10<sup>−9</sup> × 400² = 1.6 × 10<sup>−3</sup> J = 1.6 mJ.
Power in R<sub>s</sub>: P = E f<sub>s</sub> = 1.6 mJ × 20 000 = 32 W, so use a resistor rated well above 32 W.
R<sub>s</sub> ≥ V / I<sub>max</sub> = 400 V ÷ 2 A = 200 Ω.
Discharge time ≈ 3 R<sub>s</sub> C<sub>s</sub> = 3 × 200 × 20 × 10<sup>−9</sup> = 12 µs. The shortest on-time is 0.25 × 50 µs = 12.5 µs, so the capacitor just empties in time.
examples.answer: C<sub>s</sub> = 20 nF, R<sub>s</sub> = 200 Ω, 1.6 mJ per cycle and 32 W in R<sub>s</sub>; the 12 µs discharge fits inside the 12.5 µs minimum on-time.

examples.question: An SCR with a di/dt rating of 50 A/µs is switched onto a 400 V supply through a low-inductance circuit. Find the series inductance needed. A driver for an IGBT in the same cabinet switches between +15 V and −5 V through R<sub>g</sub> = 10 Ω and has R<sub>drv</sub> = 5 Ω; find its peak gate current.
steps: L<sub>s</sub> ≥ V / (di/dt) = 400 V ÷ (50 × 10<sup>6</sup> A/s) = 8 × 10<sup>−6</sup> H = 8 µH.
examples.answer: L<sub>s</sub> ≥ 8 µH; the driver's peak gate current is 1.33 A.

traps: A snubber does not save energy: the ½ C<sub>s</sub> V² f<sub>s</sub> it takes from the switch is burnt in R<sub>s</sub> (32 W in the worked example).
C<sub>s</sub> without R<sub>s</sub> dumps its charge into the switch at turn-on, limited only by stray resistance.
di/dt is a turn-on current limit fixed with a series inductor; dv/dt is an off-state voltage limit fixed with an R-C across the device. Do not swap the cures.
A fuse protects the device only if its clearing I²t is below the device's I²t rating, not because its current rating is lower.

quiz.q: Name four ratings of an SCR and what each limits.
quiz.a: V<sub>DRM</sub>: repetitive forward blocking voltage; I<sub>T(AV)</sub>: average on-state current; I<sub>TSM</sub>: one half-cycle surge current; di/dt: rate of rise of on-state current (also dv/dt, I²t).

quiz.q: Why must a turn-off snubber capacitor have a series resistor?
quiz.a: At the next turn-on the charged capacitor would discharge straight into the switch with a huge current. R<sub>s</sub> limits it to V / R<sub>s</sub> and dissipates the stored energy.

quiz.q: An R-C snubber with C<sub>s</sub> = 22 nF sits across a switch blocking 500 V at 25 kHz. Find the energy per cycle and the power in R<sub>s</sub>.
A technician removes R<sub>s</sub> from an R-C snubber to save its loss. What happens?
quiz.a: C<sub>s</sub> still limits dv/dt at turn-off, but at turn-on it discharges through the switch with only stray resistance. The peak current and di/dt become very large and can exceed the device ratings, and the ½ C<sub>s</sub> V² energy is now burnt inside the switch.

quiz.q: Why does an IGBT in a bridge need a negative gate voltage when off?
quiz.a: When the opposite IGBT turns on, the off device's collector voltage rises fast and pushes C<sub>gc</sub> dv/dt current into its gate. Without negative bias the gate can rise above threshold and turn on, shorting the DC link. −5 V to −8 V, or a Miller clamp, keeps it off.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern driver ICs include desaturation detection, soft turn-off and Miller clamps, and fast SiC and GaN devices make layout inductance critical. Search for ‘desaturation protection gate driver’ and ‘bootstrap gate drive’.
